statements.text: Cocaine hydrochloride is an ester local anesthetic that reversibly blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and prevents action-potential conduction in nerve fibers.
Its clinically important sympathomimetic effects include inhibition of catecholamine reuptake at sympathetic nerve terminals, producing local vasoconstriction and systemic cardiovascular stimulation.

Topical intranasal cocaine produces local anesthesia and vasoconstriction; systemic exposure can increase heart rate and blood pressure and is associated with concentration-dependent QTc prolongation.
The reviewed 4% nasal solution induces local anesthesia of the nasal mucosa for diagnostic procedures and surgery performed on or through the nasal cavities in adults.
Induction of local anesthesia of nasal mucous membranes for diagnostic procedures and surgeries performed on or through the nasal cavities in adults.
The most common trial adverse reactions above 1% were hypertension, tachycardia, and sinus tachycardia.
Clinically important toxicity includes seizures, increases in blood pressure and heart rate, arrhythmias, myocardial ischemia, and myocardial infarction.
Ophthalmic exposure can damage the corneal epithelium; the product is not for ophthalmic use.
The principal labeled safety domains are CNS excitation and seizure, cardiovascular stimulation or ischemia, abuse and dependence, and corneal injury after accidental ophthalmic exposure.
statements.scope: Reviewed therapeutic intranasal product; not a complete illicit-use toxicology summary

statements.text: Boxed warning: CNS stimulants including cocaine have a high potential for abuse and dependence.
Contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to cocaine hydrochloride, another ester-based local anesthetic, or any component of the product.
Monitor for seizures and clinically relevant increases in blood pressure, heart rate, and rhythm after administration.
Avoid use in patients with recent or active myocardial infarction, coronary disease, heart failure, arrhythmia, abnormal ECG, uncontrolled hypertension, or thyrotoxicosis.
The reviewed product is topical intranasal only and must not be injected or used in the eye.
Cocaine is metabolized by multiple enzymatic pathways, including plasma cholinesterase-related hydrolysis; reduced cholinesterase activity may increase toxicity risk and requires monitoring.
Systemic absorption occurs after topical nasal application, and different intranasal cocaine products should not be substituted because local and systemic exposure can differ.
Additional nasal vasoconstrictors such as epinephrine or phenylephrine can increase the risk of myocardial ischemia, infarction, and ventricular arrhythmia; avoid when possible.
Disulfiram increases cocaine exposure; CNS stimulants, tricyclic antidepressants, sympathomimetics, cholinesterase inhibitors, and monoamine-oxidase inhibitors can increase toxicity.

Monitor blood pressure, heart rate, rhythm, neurologic status, and signs of myocardial ischemia during and after administration; prolonged ECG monitoring may be needed if another vasoconstrictor is unavoidable.
Available human pregnancy data are insufficient to identify a drug-associated risk; animal studies described fetal harm at clinically relevant systemic exposures.
Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment; the label advises pumping and discarding milk for 48 hours after use.
Patients with renal impairment should be monitored for clinically relevant increases in heart rate or blood pressure.
The label does not recommend dosing the reviewed product in hepatic impairment.
Safety and effectiveness are not established in pediatric patients for the reviewed intranasal product.
Older patients may be more susceptible to cardiovascular adverse reactions and require careful monitoring.

Overdose may cause severe agitation, hyperthermia, seizures, arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, circulatory collapse, rhabdomyolysis, coma, and death; treatment is supportive and dialysis is not effective.
High-yield dual mechanism: cocaine is both an ester local anesthetic through sodium-channel blockade and an indirect sympathomimetic with marked cardiovascular toxicity.
Unlike most local anesthetics, topical cocaine also causes vasoconstriction; classic toxicity clues are hypertension, tachyarrhythmia, ischemia, seizure, and abuse potential.

statements.text: Cyclophosphamide is a prodrug activated by hepatic microsomal enzymes to alkylating metabolites that form DNA cross-links and inhibit DNA replication and cell division.

statements.text: Treatment of biopsy-proven minimal-change nephrotic syndrome in selected pediatric patients who fail or cannot tolerate corticosteroid therapy.

Serious toxicities include profound myelosuppression, severe infection/sepsis, hemorrhagic cystitis and urothelial toxicity, cardiomyopathy, pulmonary toxicity, and hepatic veno-occlusive disease.
Cyclophosphamide can cause infertility, embryo-fetal toxicity, and secondary malignancies including bladder cancer, myelodysplasia, and acute leukemia.
Rare but life-threatening reactions include severe hyponatremia/water intoxication, anaphylaxis, and severe cutaneous reactions.
Dose-limiting toxicity is primarily hematologic and urothelial, with additional cardiac, pulmonary, hepatic, reproductive, and oncogenic risks.
Contraindicated in severe hypersensitivity to cyclophosphamide or its metabolites and in urinary outflow obstruction.
Myelosuppression and severe immunosuppression require dose interruption or reduction and aggressive infection management when clinically indicated.

Avoid pregnancy and counsel about infertility and secondary malignancy risk.
Cyclophosphamide undergoes hepatic activation, principally through CYP-mediated metabolism, to active alkylating metabolites; interpatient metabolic variability can affect exposure.
Drug-related material and metabolites are eliminated mainly through the kidneys, so renal dysfunction can increase exposure and toxicity.

CYP inhibitors or inducers and drugs that add cardiotoxicity, myelosuppression, or immunosuppression can alter cyclophosphamide exposure or toxicity; live vaccines should generally be avoided during significant immunosuppression.
Monitor complete blood count with differential and platelets, signs of infection, urinalysis/hematuria, renal and hepatic function, hydration status, and cumulative cardiac or pulmonary toxicity.
Cyclophosphamide can cause fetal harm; effective contraception is required during treatment and for the label-specified period afterward.
For the reviewed injection label, breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment and for 1 week after the last dose because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in a breastfed child.
The reviewed tablet label reports cyclophosphamide in human milk and directs that the decision to discontinue nursing or the drug account for the importance of treatment to the mother.
Severe renal impairment can increase plasma cyclophosphamide concentrations; monitor for toxicity in patients with severe renal impairment.
Severe hepatic impairment may reduce conversion of cyclophosphamide to active metabolites and therefore reduce effectiveness.
The oral label includes selected pediatric minimal-change nephrotic syndrome; gonadal toxicity and secondary malignancy remain important long-term concerns.
Older adults require cautious dose selection and closer organ-function and marrow monitoring.
Overdose has no specific antidote; provide supportive care with close monitoring for marrow suppression, infection, cardiotoxicity, and urotoxicity, and consider mesna for urinary-tract protection.
Cyclophosphamide is a nitrogen-mustard alkylator and prodrug; hepatic activation yields DNA-cross-linking metabolites.
Classic testable toxicity is hemorrhagic cystitis from urotoxic metabolites; hydration and mesna are protective strategies, while myelosuppression and secondary malignancy are major systemic risks.

statements.text: Deferoxamine chelates ferric iron to form ferrioxamine, a water-soluble complex that is excreted primarily in urine and can also be excreted in bile.
Chelation reduces the pool of free or loosely bound iron available to catalyze tissue injury without meaningfully removing iron from transferrin or hemoglobin at therapeutic exposure.
Promotes iron elimination in acute iron poisoning and chronic transfusional iron overload.
Adjunctive treatment of acute iron intoxication.
Treatment of chronic iron overload due to transfusion-dependent anemias.
Common reactions include injection-site pain or swelling, rash, hypotension with overly rapid intravenous administration, and transient gastrointestinal symptoms.

Serious toxicities include auditory or ocular injury, acute renal failure or renal tubular disorders, acute respiratory distress syndrome after excessive intravenous doses, and Yersinia or mucormycosis infection.
High doses together with low ferritin levels can suppress growth in pediatric patients; monitor height and weight every 3 months.
Important organ risks involve eyes and hearing, lungs, kidneys, growth and bone, blood pressure, and infection susceptibility.
Contraindicated in severe renal disease or anuria and in hypersensitivity to deferoxamine or excipients.
Administer intravenously only by slow infusion because rapid intravenous administration can cause hypersensitivity, severe hypotension, and shock.

Monitor for auditory or ocular toxicity, renal toxicity, excessive-dose respiratory toxicity, growth suppression, and serious Yersinia or mucormycosis infection; interrupt or discontinue according to the labeled risk.
Deferoxamine can cause fetal harm; advise effective contraception during treatment and for 1 month after the last dose.
Deferoxamine is metabolized principally by plasma enzymes, although the specific pathways have not been defined.

statements.text: The ferrioxamine complex is eliminated in urine and bile; renal impairment can impair elimination and increase toxicity.

In severe chronic iron overload, high-dose vitamin C with deferoxamine can cause cardiac dysfunction; avoid the combination in cardiac failure, start vitamin C only after 1 month of regular chelation, do not exceed 200 mg/day in adults, and monitor cardiac function.
Concomitant prochlorperazine can cause temporary impairment of consciousness.
Deferoxamine-bound gallium-67 can distort scintigraphy; discontinue deferoxamine 48 hours before gallium-67 imaging.

Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment and for 1 week after the last dose.

For hepatic impairment, start dose selection at the low end of the dosing range.
Monitor growth and skeletal development during prolonged therapy; excessive dose relative to iron burden increases toxicity risk.
Older adults had an increased risk of ocular disorders; begin dose selection cautiously, generally at the low end of the range.
Overdose can cause hypotension, tachycardia, neurologic symptoms, acute visual loss, and renal dysfunction; discontinue drug and provide supportive care.

statements.text: Desmopressin is a vasopressin analogue with predominant V2-receptor activity in the renal collecting duct, increasing water reabsorption and reducing urine output.
In responsive patients with mild hemophilia A or type 1 von Willebrand disease, desmopressin injection increases plasma factor VIII activity and can improve hemostasis.
Antidiuretic potency is enhanced relative to vasopressin while vasopressor activity is reduced; hemostatic response is patient- and disease-specific.
Reduces polyuria and polydipsia in central diabetes insipidus and can transiently improve hemostasis in responsive bleeding disorders.
Intranasal antidiuretic replacement therapy for central diabetes insipidus in adults and pediatric patients 4 years of age and older.
Injection management of central diabetes insipidus, including temporary polyuria and polydipsia after head trauma or pituitary-region surgery.
Injection hemostatic treatment for hemophilia A with factor VIII coagulant activity above 5% and no factor VIII antibodies, when an adequate response is demonstrated.
statements.scope: Desmopressin injection; selected responsive hemophilia A

statements.text: Common reactions include headache, flushing, nausea, abdominal discomfort, nasal symptoms with intranasal use, and transient blood-pressure changes.
Severe hyponatremia and water intoxication can cause seizure, coma, respiratory arrest, and death.
Serious hypersensitivity and thrombosis have been reported; hemostatic use requires attention to blood-pressure and thrombotic risk.

statements.text: For nasal spray, contraindications include hypersensitivity, creatinine clearance below 50 mL/min, and hyponatremia or a history of hyponatremia.

For injection, contraindications additionally include SIADH, polydipsia, loop diuretics, systemic or inhaled glucocorticoids, acute illnesses causing fluid/electrolyte imbalance, heart failure, and uncontrolled hypertension.
Restrict fluid intake to reduce the risk of water intoxication and hyponatremia.
The injection is contraindicated during illnesses that can cause fluid or electrolyte imbalance and in several other high-risk states specified in section 4.

Do not assume hemostatic benefit in severe type 1 von Willebrand disease or when abnormal molecular forms of von Willebrand factor are present; type IIB von Willebrand disease can carry thrombotic risk with desmopressin.
After intranasal administration, desmopressin has a biphasic elimination profile with initial and terminal half-lives of 7.8 and 75.5 minutes, respectively.
Desmopressin is mainly excreted in urine; after a single 2-mcg intravenous dose, terminal half-life and exposure increased progressively as renal function declined.
statements.scope: Renal-impairment study using a 2-mcg intravenous dose; the nasal label notes this exposure is about 20 times that of a 10-mcg nasal dose

statements.text: Bioavailability and exposure differ substantially by route; nasal and injectable products are not dose-equivalent and must not be interchanged by microgram-for-microgram assumptions.

Concomitant drugs that increase water-intoxication or hyponatremia risk—including tricyclic antidepressants, SSRIs, opioids, NSAIDs, lamotrigine, oxybutynin, and carbamazepine—require more frequent sodium monitoring.
The injection label additionally identifies thiazide diuretics and sulfonylureas, particularly chlorpropamide, among drugs requiring closer sodium monitoring.
For injection, ensure serum sodium is normal before starting or resuming treatment, recheck within 7 days and at approximately 1 month, then periodically according to risk.
For nasal spray, monitor response with urine volume and osmolality, assess serum sodium and plasma osmolality as needed, and maintain appropriate fluid restriction.

For hemostatic use, confirm and monitor the response with factor VIII coagulant activity, activated partial thromboplastin time, ristocetin cofactor activity, and von Willebrand factor antigen as applicable, together with bleeding control and sodium status.
Available pregnancy data have not identified a drug-associated risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or other adverse maternal or fetal outcomes.
Desmopressin is present in human milk in low amounts; consider infant and maternal factors.
Moderate-to-severe renal impairment is contraindicated because reduced clearance increases hyponatremia risk.
For the reviewed nasal spray, central-diabetes-insipidus use is established from age 4 years.
For the reviewed injection, hemophilia A and type 1 von Willebrand disease use is established from age 3 months, while central-diabetes-insipidus use is established from age 12 years.
Older adults have higher hyponatremia risk and require cautious selection and closer sodium monitoring.

Overdose produces prolonged antidiuresis, fluid retention, hyponatremia, and neurologic deterioration; reduce or stop treatment, restrict fluid, and manage sodium abnormalities under close monitoring.

Desmopressin is a V2-predominant vasopressin analogue used for central diabetes insipidus; its injection can raise factor VIII activity and improve hemostasis in responsive mild hemophilia A or type 1 vWD.
The signature toxicity is dilutional hyponatremia from water retention, so fluid restriction and sodium monitoring are essential; only the reviewed injection product carries a boxed warning.

Opioids, alcohol, and other centrally acting depressants can produce additive sedation and respiratory depression.

TNF blockade reduces inflammatory-cell infiltration and inflammatory mediators in responsive immune-mediated disease.
Intravenous induction and maintenance regimens can reduce disease activity and support remission or structural benefit across labeled gastrointestinal, rheumatologic, and dermatologic indications.
Moderately to severely active Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis in adults, with labeled pediatric use from age 6 years for both conditions.
Moderately to severely active rheumatoid arthritis in combination with methotrexate.
Active ankylosing spondylitis and psoriatic arthritis.
Chronic severe plaque psoriasis in appropriate adult candidates for systemic therapy.
Common adverse reactions include infections, infusion-related reactions, headache, and abdominal pain.

Serious risks include tuberculosis and other opportunistic infections, malignancy, hepatitis B reactivation, severe hepatotoxicity, worsening heart failure, cytopenias, demyelinating disease, and severe infusion or hypersensitivity reactions.
Hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma has occurred, particularly in adolescent or young adult males with inflammatory bowel disease receiving TNF blockers with thiopurines.
Major safety domains are infection, malignancy, infusion immunogenicity, hepatic injury, cardiac failure, hematologic abnormalities, and neurologic demyelination.

Boxed warning: TNF blockers increase the risk of serious infections that can lead to hospitalization or death, including tuberculosis, bacterial sepsis, invasive fungal infection, and other opportunistic infections.
Boxed warning: lymphoma and other malignancies, including fatal cases in children and adolescents, have been reported with TNF blockers.

Doses greater than 5 mg/kg are contraindicated in moderate or severe heart failure; the drug is also contraindicated after severe hypersensitivity to infliximab, murine proteins, or product components.
Test for latent and active tuberculosis before treatment and monitor for TB and other infection during therapy; discontinue for serious infection or sepsis.
Screen patients at risk for hepatitis B and monitor carriers during and after therapy for reactivation.
Avoid use in moderate or severe heart failure when prohibited by dose and discontinue if new or worsening heart-failure symptoms occur.

Bring patients up to date with vaccines before treatment when feasible; do not give live vaccines or therapeutic infectious agents during REMICADE treatment, and follow the infant-exposure restriction after in-utero exposure.
The median terminal half-life is approximately 7.7 to 9.5 days after intravenous administration.
Formation of antibodies to infliximab can increase clearance, reduce serum concentrations, and increase infusion-reaction risk.
Concomitant anakinra, abatacept, or another biologic used for the same condition is not recommended because serious infection risk increases without established added benefit.
Live vaccines and therapeutic infectious agents should not be given concurrently with REMICADE.

Before and during treatment assess TB and infection risk, hepatitis B status, infusion reactions, heart-failure symptoms, liver tests when clinically indicated, and blood counts for suspected cytopenia.

Infliximab crosses the placenta and can be detected in exposed infants; do not administer live vaccines to an exposed infant for at least 6 months after birth unless the infant's serum infliximab level is undetectable.
Infliximab is present at low levels in human milk; use requires balancing maternal need and infant risk.
Labeled pediatric indications include Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis from age 6 years; malignancy and serious infection warnings are especially important.
Serious infections were more frequent in patients 65 years and older; use greater caution.
Single doses up to 20 mg/kg have been administered without direct toxic effect in reported experience; monitor and provide supportive care after excessive exposure.
Infliximab is a chimeric anti-TNF-α monoclonal antibody given intravenously; screen for TB and hepatitis B before treatment.
High-yield anti-TNF hazards include serious infection, reactivation of latent TB/HBV, malignancy, demyelination, worsening heart failure, and avoidance of live vaccines.

statements.text: Latanoprost is a prostaglandin F2α analogue and an isopropyl-ester prodrug that is hydrolyzed in the cornea to an active acid; it lowers intraocular pressure mainly by increasing uveoscleral aqueous-humor outflow.
Intraocular-pressure reduction begins about 3 to 4 hours after administration, reaches a maximum after 8 to 12 hours, and persists for at least 24 hours after a single dose.
Once-daily topical administration lowers elevated intraocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension.
Reduction of elevated intraocular pressure in patients with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension.

Ocular adverse reactions reported in 5% to 15% of patients included blurred vision, burning or stinging, conjunctival hyperemia, foreign-body sensation, itching, increased iris pigmentation, and punctate epithelial keratopathy.
Clinically important ocular risks include macular edema, intraocular inflammation, and reactivation of herpetic keratitis.
Increased iris pigmentation may be permanent; the long-term consequences of the pigment change are unknown.
Adverse effects are predominantly ocular and periocular, including pigmentation, eyelash changes, irritation, inflammation, and macular edema in susceptible eyes.
The reviewed U.S. label contains no boxed warning.
Contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to latanoprost, benzalkonium chloride, or another component.
Counsel that increased brown iris pigmentation may be permanent and that eyelid skin and eyelash changes can occur.
Use caution in patients at risk for macular edema, with active intraocular inflammation, or with a history of herpetic keratitis.
Remove contact lenses before instillation and wait at least 15 minutes before reinsertion because the preservative can be absorbed by soft lenses.
Multidose ophthalmic containers have been associated with bacterial keratitis after inadvertent contamination; avoid contact between the dispensing tip and the eye or surrounding structures.
IOP lowering begins approximately 3 to 4 hours after a dose.
The pressure-lowering effect persists for at least 24 hours.
After corneal absorption, the ester prodrug is hydrolyzed to active latanoprost acid and is then metabolized largely by fatty-acid beta oxidation.
In-vitro studies found precipitation when latanoprost was mixed with thimerosal-containing eye drops; administer such medicines at least 5 minutes apart.
Using two or more prostaglandins or prostaglandin analogues together can paradoxically raise intraocular pressure; multiple agents in this class are not recommended.
Monitor intraocular pressure, visual symptoms, ocular inflammation, macular edema in at-risk patients, and pigment or eyelash changes.

Human pregnancy data are inadequate to define drug-associated risk; animal studies reported malformations, embryofetal lethality, and spontaneous abortion after systemic exposure at clinically relevant multiples.
Use caution during lactation because it is unknown whether latanoprost or metabolites are present in human milk under the reviewed label.
Safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients have not been established under the reviewed label.
No overall safety or effectiveness difference was observed between older and younger adults.
The reviewed label recommends symptomatic treatment for overdose; systemic high-dose exposure has produced abdominal pain, dizziness, fatigue, flushing, nausea, and sweating.
Latanoprost is a prostaglandin F2α analogue prodrug that lowers IOP mainly by increasing uveoscleral outflow.
Classic adverse effects are permanent iris darkening, eyelid-skin pigmentation, eyelash growth, conjunctival hyperemia, and possible macular edema.

statements.text: Metoclopramide stimulates upper gastrointestinal motility, appears to sensitize tissue to acetylcholine, increases lower-esophageal-sphincter tone, and accelerates gastric emptying without stimulating secretions.
Its antiemetic effect is attributed to central and peripheral dopamine-receptor antagonism, including activity at the chemoreceptor trigger zone.

In a primary experimental study, metoclopramide produced a 5-HT4-like agonist response in ileum and increased gastric emptying; this supports the legacy 5-HT4 prokinetic classification but is not itself a human indication or dosing source.
Prokinetic effects can be abolished by anticholinergic drugs and do not require intact vagal innervation.
Route-specific products provide prokinetic therapy for diabetic gastroparesis and antiemetic therapy in selected chemotherapy, postoperative, and procedural settings.
Oral treatment for 4 to 12 weeks of symptomatic, documented gastroesophageal reflux that fails conventional therapy in adults.
Relief of symptoms associated with acute and recurrent diabetic gastroparesis in adults, with oral or injection use selected according to clinical circumstances.
Injection prevention of nausea and vomiting associated with emetogenic cancer chemotherapy in adults.
Injection prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting in adults when nasogastric suction is undesirable.
Injection facilitation of small-bowel intubation in adults and pediatric patients when the tube does not pass the pylorus with conventional maneuvers.

statements.text: Injection facilitation of radiologic examination of the upper gastrointestinal tract in adults when delayed gastric emptying interferes with the examination.
The most common adverse reactions are restlessness, drowsiness, fatigue, and lassitude.
Serious reactions include tardive dyskinesia, acute dystonia, parkinsonism, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, depression or suicidality, hypertension, and fluid retention.
Methemoglobinemia and sulfhemoglobinemia are rare but important, particularly in neonates and patients with NADH cytochrome-b5 reductase deficiency.
Dose- and duration-related neurologic toxicity dominates, with additional psychiatric, cardiovascular, endocrine, and hematologic risks.
Boxed warning: metoclopramide can cause tardive dyskinesia, often irreversible; avoid treatment longer than 12 weeks except in rare circumstances.

Contraindications include prior tardive dyskinesia or dystonic reaction, gastrointestinal hemorrhage/obstruction/perforation, pheochromocytoma or other catecholamine-releasing paraganglioma, epilepsy, and hypersensitivity.
Stop therapy if tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, or clinically important extrapyramidal symptoms occur.
Avoid use with other drugs likely to cause tardive dyskinesia or extrapyramidal reactions and avoid alcohol or other CNS depressants when possible.
Pharmacologic effects begin within about 1 to 3 minutes after intravenous dosing, 10 to 15 minutes after intramuscular dosing, and 30 to 60 minutes after oral dosing.
Pharmacologic effects persist approximately 1 to 2 hours.
The mean elimination half-life in people with normal renal function is approximately 5 to 6 hours and is prolonged by renal impairment.
Metoclopramide and metabolites are eliminated primarily in urine; reduced renal function requires dose reduction.
Antipsychotics increase tardive-dyskinesia, extrapyramidal, and neuroleptic-malignant-syndrome risk; concomitant use should be avoided.
Strong CYP2D6 inhibitors increase metoclopramide exposure and require dose reduction; examples in the label include fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion, and quinidine.
Metoclopramide alters absorption of drugs affected by gastric emptying and can reduce digoxin exposure or increase cyclosporine exposure.
Monitor treatment duration, involuntary movements, dystonia or akathisia, parkinsonism, mental status, blood pressure, and renal function for dose adjustment.

Available published data have not identified a major-drug-associated risk of birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal/fetal outcomes; neonatal extrapyramidal signs can occur after late exposure.
Metoclopramide is present in human milk and exposed infants should be monitored for gastrointestinal or extrapyramidal effects.
Reduce dosage when creatinine clearance is 60 mL/min or less because systemic exposure and adverse-reaction risk increase.
Reduce oral dosage in moderate or severe hepatic impairment; hepatic metabolism and fluid-retention risk affect use.
Metoclopramide tablets are not recommended in pediatric patients because of tardive-dyskinesia and other extrapyramidal risks and because effectiveness is not established.
The reviewed injection label includes pediatric small-bowel intubation; other pediatric injection uses are not established, and neonates have increased methemoglobinemia risk.
Older adults have increased risk of tardive dyskinesia and may require lower doses based on renal function.
Overdose may cause drowsiness, disorientation, extrapyramidal reactions, and methemoglobinemia; stop drug and provide supportive or symptom-directed treatment.
Metoclopramide is a dopamine-receptor antagonist antiemetic with prokinetic activity; major exam toxicities are acute dystonia, parkinsonism, hyperprolactinemia, and tardive dyskinesia.

Metoclopramide has experimentally demonstrated 5-HT4-like agonist prokinetic activity; current U.S. labels emphasize dopamine antagonism and acetylcholine sensitization, so the receptor-level teaching point remains distinct from labeled indications.

statements.text: Octreotide is a synthetic somatostatin analogue that inhibits growth hormone and multiple gastroenteropancreatic hormones, including glucagon, insulin, gastrin, vasoactive intestinal peptide, and serotonin.

Hormone suppression lowers GH/IGF-1 in acromegaly and reduces severe secretory diarrhea or flushing from carcinoid and VIP-secreting tumors.
Reduction of growth hormone and IGF-1 in acromegaly when response to or eligibility for surgery, pituitary irradiation, or maximally tolerated bromocriptine is inadequate.
Treatment of severe diarrhea and flushing episodes associated with metastatic carcinoid tumors.
Treatment of profuse watery diarrhea associated with vasoactive intestinal peptide tumors.

In acromegaly trials, adverse reactions occurring in more than 10% included gallbladder abnormalities, sinus bradycardia, diarrhea, loose stools, nausea, abdominal discomfort, hyperglycemia, and hypothyroidism.

Clinically important risks include bradycardia or conduction abnormalities, cholelithiasis and its complications, hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia, thyroid dysfunction, and severe steatorrhea or malabsorption.
Pancreatitis can occur in association with gallbladder disease or after therapy changes.
Clinically important effects involve gastrointestinal and biliary function, glucose regulation, cardiac rate or conduction, thyroid function, nutrition, and injection sites.
The reviewed U.S. label contains no boxed warning.
Contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to octreotide or product components.
Monitor for bradycardia or conduction abnormalities, especially when other drugs that slow heart rate are used.
Monitor for gallstones and complications; discontinue when complications are suspected and treat appropriately.
Monitor glucose, thyroid function during chronic therapy, stool or nutritional symptoms of fat malabsorption, and vitamin B12 when clinically indicated.
After subcutaneous injection, peak concentrations occur at about 0.4 hours.
The apparent plasma half-life is approximately 1.7 to 1.9 hours, substantially longer than native somatostatin.
About one-third of an injected dose is excreted unchanged in urine, and clearance is reduced in renal failure requiring dialysis and in cirrhosis.
Octreotide can reduce cyclosporine absorption and may require cyclosporine dose adjustment.
Insulin and oral hypoglycemic doses may need adjustment because octreotide alters glucose-regulatory hormones.
It increases bromocriptine bioavailability and can alter clearance of drugs metabolized by CYP enzymes; use caution with narrow-therapeutic-index CYP3A4 substrates.
Concomitant drugs that cause bradycardia can have additive effects; dosage adjustment may be necessary.
Discontinue immediate-release octreotide at least 24 hours before each lutetium Lu-177 dotatate dose.
Monitor clinical symptoms and indication-specific biomarkers, heart rate or ECG when at risk, gallbladder complications, glucose, thyroid function, nutrition or fat malabsorption, and vitamin B12.
Available case data are insufficient to establish a drug-associated pregnancy risk; restored fertility from GH normalization may lead to unintended pregnancy.
There are no data on octreotide in human milk, infant effects, or milk production; balance benefits of breastfeeding and maternal treatment.
Half-life may increase and clearance decrease in renal impairment, particularly in dialysis; maintenance dosage may require adjustment.
In cirrhosis, half-life increases and dosage adjustment may be required.
Safety and effectiveness have not been established in pediatric patients under the reviewed label.
Older adults may have prolonged half-life; dose selection should be cautious and reflect organ function and comorbidity.

Reported overdose manifestations include arrhythmia, complete atrioventricular block, hypotension, cardiac arrest, brain hypoxia, pancreatitis, hepatic steatosis or hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, flushing, diarrhea, lethargy, weakness, and weight loss; treatment is symptomatic.
Octreotide is a long-acting somatostatin analogue used for acromegaly and secretory diarrhea or flushing from carcinoid and VIPoma.
High-yield adverse effects are gallstones, steatorrhea or malabsorption, glucose abnormalities, bradycardia, hypothyroidism, and reduced vitamin B12.

statements.text: Panitumumab is a recombinant human IgG2 kappa monoclonal antibody that binds the extracellular domain of EGFR, blocks ligand-induced receptor activation, and inhibits downstream signaling in susceptible tumor cells.

Clinical benefit from EGFR blockade in metastatic colorectal cancer is strongly dependent on tumor RAS genotype; RAS-mutant tumors generally lack benefit except for the specifically labeled KRAS G12C combination with sotorasib.
Panitumumab provides biomarker-directed treatment for metastatic colorectal cancer as monotherapy or in labeled combinations.
Treatment of adult patients with wild-type RAS metastatic colorectal cancer in the label-defined monotherapy or combination settings, with RAS status established by an FDA-approved test.
Treatment of adult patients with KRAS G12C-mutated metastatic colorectal cancer in combination with sotorasib after prior fluoropyrimidine-, oxaliplatin-, and irinotecan-based chemotherapy.

Common adverse reactions are dominated by dermatologic toxicity, including rash, acneiform dermatitis, pruritus, erythema, paronychia, dry skin, and fissures; diarrhea, fatigue, nausea, and electrolyte abnormalities also occur.

Serious risks include severe dermatologic and soft-tissue toxicity with infectious complications, infusion reactions, severe electrolyte depletion, acute renal failure from diarrhea or dehydration, interstitial lung disease, ocular injury, and embryo-fetal toxicity.
Pulmonary fibrosis or interstitial lung disease, including fatal cases, is a rare but important toxicity.
EGFR-related skin, nail, ocular, gastrointestinal, and electrolyte toxicities predominate, with additional pulmonary, renal, and infusion risks.
Boxed warning: dermatologic toxicities occur in most patients and can be severe; monitor for inflammatory or infectious sequelae and apply dose-interruption or discontinuation criteria.
The reviewed U.S. label lists no formal contraindications.
Do not use for RAS-mutant or unknown-RAS metastatic colorectal cancer outside the specifically labeled KRAS G12C plus sotorasib setting.
Monitor magnesium and calcium during treatment and for up to 8 weeks after completion because progressive hypomagnesemia and associated electrolyte abnormalities can occur.
Withhold or discontinue for severe infusion reaction, interstitial lung disease, serious ocular toxicity, or recurrent severe dermatologic toxicity according to label criteria.
Limit sun exposure and use sunscreen or protective clothing during treatment and for 2 months after the final dose.
The elimination half-life is approximately 7.5 days over the labeled dose range.
Panitumumab displays nonlinear pharmacokinetics at lower doses, with EGFR-mediated clearance becoming saturated as dose increases.
Panitumumab with bevacizumab-containing chemotherapy increased toxicity and mortality and is not indicated; combination-specific management with sotorasib must follow both labels.

Confirm tumor RAS or KRAS G12C status as required; monitor skin and nails, infection, magnesium/calcium/potassium, diarrhea and hydration, renal function, infusion reactions, respiratory symptoms, and ocular symptoms.
EGFR blockade can cause fetal harm; advise effective contraception during treatment and for at least 2 months after the last dose.
Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment and for 2 months after the last dose.
Safety and effectiveness have not been established in pediatric patients.
No overall effectiveness difference was observed by age, but combination regimens can have age-related toxicity differences requiring clinical judgment.
Doses up to approximately twice the recommended therapeutic dose have produced skin toxicity, diarrhea, dehydration, and fatigue.

statements.text: Pembrolizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds PD-1 and blocks its interaction with PD-L1 and PD-L2, releasing PD-1-mediated inhibition of antitumor T-cell responses.
PD-1 blockade can restore antitumor immunity but can also break peripheral tolerance and cause immune-mediated inflammation in essentially any organ system.
Pembrolizumab can be used as monotherapy or in tumor-specific combinations, with eligibility determined by cancer type, stage, prior therapy, and sometimes PD-L1, MSI/dMMR, TMB, or other biomarkers.

Current labeled indications include melanoma, NSCLC, malignant pleural mesothelioma, head and neck squamous-cell cancer, classical Hodgkin lymphoma, primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma, and urothelial cancer in indication-specific settings.
Biomarker-defined indications include MSI-high or mismatch-repair-deficient cancers and colorectal cancer, tumor-mutational-burden-high cancer, and selected PD-L1-defined settings.

Additional current indications include gastric, esophageal, cervical, hepatocellular, biliary-tract, Merkel-cell, renal-cell, endometrial, cutaneous squamous-cell, triple-negative breast, and ovarian cancers, each with label-specific stage, biomarker, and combination requirements.

Common reactions vary by regimen; monotherapy commonly causes fatigue, musculoskeletal pain, decreased appetite, pruritus, diarrhea, nausea, rash, fever, cough, dyspnea, constipation, and abdominal pain, while combination partners add substantial regimen-specific toxicity.

Severe or fatal immune-mediated reactions include pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis, endocrinopathies, nephritis, severe skin reactions, neurologic syndromes, myocarditis, and other organ inflammation; infusion reactions and allogeneic-transplant complications also occur.
Rare immune toxicities can involve the nervous system, heart, blood, eye, musculoskeletal system, or transplanted organs and may appear after treatment stops.
Because PD-1 blockade can affect any organ system, new symptoms require evaluation for immune-mediated toxicity rather than attribution only to the underlying cancer.
The reviewed U.S. label contains no boxed warning.
The reviewed U.S. label lists no formal contraindications.

Identify immune-mediated toxicity early, exclude alternative causes including infection, and withhold or permanently discontinue according to organ and grade; systemic corticosteroids are often required.
Monitor for infusion-related reactions and stop permanently for severe or life-threatening reactions.
Allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation before or after PD-1 blockade can cause severe or fatal complications.
Use with a thalidomide analogue plus dexamethasone in multiple myeloma outside controlled trials increased mortality and is not recommended.
The terminal half-life is approximately 22 days at steady state.

Pembrolizumab clearance decreases over the first months of treatment and then remains approximately stable; the label describes fixed-dose exposure and population covariates without asserting a conventional CYP-metabolism pathway.

At baseline and periodically monitor liver enzymes, creatinine, and thyroid function, and assess clinical symptoms for pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis, endocrinopathy, nephritis, skin toxicity, neurologic toxicity, and other immune-mediated disease.
Based on PD-1 pathway biology, pembrolizumab can cause fetal harm; advise effective contraception during treatment and for 4 months after the last dose.
Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment and for 4 months after the last dose.
An estimated glomerular-filtration rate of at least 15 mL/min/1.73 m² had no clinically significant effect on pembrolizumab clearance in population pharmacokinetic analysis.
Mild or moderate hepatic impairment had no clinically significant effect on pembrolizumab clearance; the effect of severe hepatic impairment is unknown.
Pediatric approval is indication-specific, including selected melanoma and lymphoma populations; safety and effectiveness are not established for every adult indication.
No overall safety or effectiveness difference was identified for many studied indications, but data are regimen- and cancer-specific.
Pembrolizumab binds PD-1 and blocks its interactions with PD-L1 and PD-L2, releasing PD-1-mediated inhibition of antitumor T-cell responses.
High-yield monitoring includes thyroid function, liver enzymes, creatinine, pulmonary symptoms, diarrhea or colitis, glucose/endocrine symptoms, skin, and neurologic findings.

statements.text: Glucocorticoids have profound and varied metabolic effects and modify the body's immune responses; labeled effects include anti-inflammatory activity, altered carbohydrate and protein metabolism, sodium retention, potassium loss, and HPA-axis suppression.
Systemic prednisolone rapidly suppresses inflammatory and immune manifestations but does not treat the underlying cause and can mask infection.

Systemic corticosteroid therapy for label-listed endocrine, rheumatic, collagen, dermatologic, allergic, ophthalmic, respiratory, hematologic, neoplastic, edematous, gastrointestinal, and other inflammatory conditions.
The specific dose and duration are disease- and patient-dependent and should be individualized to the lowest effective exposure.
Common exposure-related effects include increased appetite, dyspepsia, mood or sleep change, hyperglycemia, fluid retention, hypertension, and Cushingoid appearance.

Serious risks include severe infection, adrenal suppression or crisis, gastrointestinal ulcer or bleeding, osteoporosis and fractures, psychiatric reactions, ocular injury, myopathy, hypertension, and major metabolic disturbance.
The label lists uncommon but clinically important reactions including anaphylactoid or hypersensitivity reactions, pancreatitis, and aseptic necrosis of the femoral or humeral head.

Toxicity is multisystem and increases with dose and duration, particularly affecting infection risk, endocrine metabolism, bone, muscle, gastrointestinal tract, eye, cardiovascular system, and mental status.
The reviewed U.S. label contains no boxed warning.
Contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to prednisolone or any product component.
Systemic corticosteroids suppress immunity, increase susceptibility to infection, may reactivate latent infections, and can mask infection signs.
Do not stop prolonged or high-dose therapy abruptly; taper when appropriate to reduce adrenal insufficiency and withdrawal.
Use the lowest effective dose and monitor for hyperglycemia, hypertension or fluid retention, gastrointestinal injury, osteoporosis, psychiatric symptoms, growth effects, and cataract or glaucoma.
Avoid live vaccines during immunosuppressive doses and manage exposure to varicella or measles promptly.
Prednisolone is metabolized primarily in the liver and is susceptible to clinically important CYP3A-mediated interactions.
Metabolites are eliminated mainly in urine.
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors can increase corticosteroid exposure and inducers can reduce exposure; monitor and adjust when clinically necessary.
NSAIDs or aspirin can increase gastrointestinal toxicity; diuretics can worsen hypokalemia; antidiabetic therapy may need adjustment; anticoagulant effect can change.
Live vaccines are generally avoided during immunosuppressive corticosteroid therapy.

Monitor clinical response and infection, blood pressure, weight and edema, glucose, electrolytes, bone risk, growth in children, mood or sleep, ocular pressure or cataract risk, and adrenal suppression during tapering.
Use in pregnancy requires balancing maternal need and fetal risk; prolonged or repeated exposure may affect fetal growth and newborn adrenal function.

Systemically administered corticosteroids appear in human milk and may suppress growth or endogenous corticosteroid production in a breastfed infant; use clinical judgment when deciding whether to continue nursing or treatment.
Renal disease can amplify sodium and fluid retention; monitor volume status and electrolytes.
Long-term systemic corticosteroids can suppress growth; monitor growth and minimize chronic exposure where possible.

Acute overdose is usually managed supportively; chronic excessive exposure causes hypercortisolism, metabolic effects, immunosuppression, and HPA-axis suppression and requires gradual reduction rather than abrupt cessation.
Prednisolone is a systemic glucocorticoid; major long-term hazards include infection, hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, adrenal suppression, cataract or glaucoma, myopathy, and psychiatric effects.

statements.text: Ranitidine competitively and reversibly blocks histamine H2 receptors on gastric parietal cells, reducing basal and stimulated gastric-acid secretion and pepsin output.
Acid suppression reduces both volume and hydrogen-ion concentration of gastric secretion with minimal anticholinergic activity.
Current reformulated ranitidine remains an H2-receptor antagonist for acid-related gastrointestinal disease.

The 2020 U.S. market withdrawal applied to then-marketed ranitidine products because NDMA could rise during storage; it should not be misrepresented as the present status of the 2025 reformulated product.
Short-term treatment and maintenance after healing of duodenal ulcer and benign gastric ulcer.
Treatment of pathological hypersecretory conditions such as Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and systemic mastocytosis.
Treatment of GERD and treatment or maintenance of healing of endoscopically diagnosed erosive esophagitis.

Headache is the adverse reaction most clearly related to ranitidine; constipation, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal discomfort or pain were reported but were not always clearly different from background rates.
Serious reported reactions include hepatitis or hepatic failure, blood dyscrasias, anaphylaxis, angioedema, arrhythmia, pancreatitis, and acute interstitial nephritis.
Rare reversible confusion, agitation, depression, or hallucinations occur mainly in severely ill older adults; acute porphyria attacks have also been reported.

Most patients tolerate ranitidine, but renal accumulation, CNS effects in frail older adults, hepatic injury, hematologic abnormalities, hypersensitivity, and cardiac conduction events remain clinically important.
The reviewed current U.S. label contains no boxed warning.
Contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to ranitidine or product ingredients.
Symptom improvement does not exclude gastric malignancy.
Adjust dose for renal impairment, use caution with hepatic dysfunction, and avoid in patients with a history of acute porphyria.
Follow the reformulated product storage and 90-day-after-opening discard instructions to preserve product quality.
Symptomatic relief in GERD and erosive esophagitis commonly occurs within 24 hours under the reviewed label.
The elimination half-life is approximately 2.5 to 3 hours in people with normal renal function and is prolonged in renal impairment and older adults.
Ranitidine is substantially eliminated by the kidneys; dosage adjustment is required with impaired renal function.

The reformulated product has storage controls intended to address prior NDMA formation concerns: keep tablets in the original tightly closed container, protect from moisture, retain desiccant, and discard unused tablets 90 days after first opening or by expiry, whichever comes first.
High ranitidine doses can reduce renal tubular secretion of procainamide and increase procainamide and N-acetylprocainamide concentrations.
Reports of altered prothrombin time with warfarin are inconsistent; closely monitor prothrombin time during concomitant treatment.

By increasing gastric pH, ranitidine can reduce absorption of medicines such as atazanavir, delavirdine, gefitinib, and ketoconazole; apply the affected product's separation or avoidance instructions.
Ranitidine increased glipizide exposure in reported studies; monitor for hypoglycemia when the drugs are combined.
Ranitidine increased exposure to orally administered midazolam and triazolam; monitor for excessive or prolonged sedation.
Monitor symptom response and alarm features, renal function for dose adjustment, hepatic symptoms, mental status in frail older adults, and adherence to product storage and discard instructions.
Use in pregnancy only when clearly needed under the reviewed label.
Ranitidine is secreted in human milk; use caution in nursing patients.
Reduce dose or extend the interval in renal impairment because the drug is substantially renally excreted.
Use caution in hepatic dysfunction because ranitidine undergoes hepatic metabolism and rare serious liver injury has occurred.
Pediatric use in the current reviewed tablet label is not comprehensively established for all listed conditions; use product- and age-specific information.
Older adults are more likely to have reduced renal function and may be more susceptible to CNS adverse effects; choose dose cautiously and consider renal monitoring.
Overdose is managed with removal of unabsorbed drug when appropriate, clinical monitoring, and supportive therapy; hemodialysis can remove circulating ranitidine.
Ranitidine is an H2-receptor antagonist, not a proton-pump inhibitor; it reduces gastric acid by blocking parietal-cell H2 receptors.

Regulatory-history pearl: legacy products were withdrawn in the U.S. on April 1, 2020 because NDMA could increase during storage, but FDA approved reformulated tablets on November 24, 2025 after new safety testing and manufacturing controls.

statements.text: Salmeterol is a selective long-acting beta2-adrenergic receptor agonist that activates adenylyl cyclase, raises cyclic AMP in airway smooth muscle, and produces bronchodilation.
Its lipophilic side chain contributes to prolonged receptor-region residence and bronchodilation lasting approximately 12 hours.
Twice-daily inhaled salmeterol provides maintenance bronchodilation but does not relieve acute bronchospasm and must not be used as asthma monotherapy without an inhaled corticosteroid.

Maintenance treatment of asthma and prevention of bronchospasm only as concomitant therapy with an inhaled corticosteroid in patients aged 4 years and older who are not adequately controlled on the corticosteroid alone.
Prevention of exercise-induced bronchospasm in patients aged 4 years and older.
Long-term twice-daily maintenance treatment of bronchospasm associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, including chronic bronchitis and emphysema.
In asthma trials, common reactions included headache, influenza, nasal or sinus congestion, pharyngitis, rhinitis, tracheitis or bronchitis, cough, and musculoskeletal pain.
In COPD trials, common reactions included headache, musculoskeletal pain, throat irritation, and respiratory infection; beta2-agonist effects can also include tremor, palpitations, and tachycardia.

Serious risks include asthma-related death when used without an inhaled corticosteroid, paradoxical bronchospasm, clinically significant cardiovascular effects or arrhythmias, immediate hypersensitivity, hypokalemia, and hyperglycemia.
Immediate hypersensitivity can occur, and the lactose-containing dry-powder device can trigger reactions in patients with severe milk-protein allergy.
Adverse effects reflect excessive beta2 stimulation, airway hypersensitivity, paradoxical bronchospasm, and asthma-safety risk from inappropriate monotherapy.
Boxed warning: LABA monotherapy without inhaled corticosteroid increases asthma-related death; SEREVENT DISKUS asthma use must be additional to inhaled corticosteroid therapy.
Contraindicated as asthma monotherapy without an inhaled corticosteroid and in patients with severe hypersensitivity to milk proteins or any component.

Do not initiate salmeterol during rapidly deteriorating or acutely life-threatening asthma or COPD, and do not use it as primary treatment for status asthmaticus or another acute episode requiring intensive measures; provide a short-acting inhaled beta2 agonist for rescue.
Do not exceed the recommended dose or combine with another LABA because excessive sympathomimetic and cardiovascular toxicity can occur.

Stop salmeterol immediately and institute alternative therapy if paradoxical bronchospasm occurs; evaluate immediate hypersensitivity separately and monitor susceptible patients for cardiovascular effects, hypokalemia, and hyperglycemia.
Bronchodilation begins more slowly than with a short-acting beta2 agonist, so salmeterol is not a rescue medication.
A single inhaled dose provides clinically significant bronchodilation for about 12 hours.
Salmeterol is metabolized predominantly by CYP3A4.
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ketoconazole can markedly increase systemic salmeterol exposure and cardiovascular risk; concomitant use is not recommended.
Monoamine-oxidase inhibitors and tricyclic antidepressants can potentiate cardiovascular effects; beta blockers can antagonize bronchodilation and provoke bronchospasm.
Non-potassium-sparing diuretics can worsen beta-agonist-associated hypokalemia or ECG changes.

Monitor asthma or COPD control, rescue-inhaler use, acute deterioration, heart rate and symptoms of arrhythmia, potassium or glucose in susceptible patients, and adherence to inhaled corticosteroid in asthma.
Available data from published epidemiologic studies and case reports have not established a drug-associated risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes.
It is unknown whether salmeterol is present in human milk; balance breastfeeding benefits, maternal need, and potential infant effects.
Hepatic impairment may increase systemic exposure; monitor for adverse effects.
Labeled asthma and exercise-induced bronchospasm use begins at age 4 years; a fixed ICS/LABA combination is ordinarily preferred in children who need a LABA to support adherence to both components.
No overall effectiveness difference was observed, but older adults may be more susceptible to beta-agonist cardiovascular effects.

Overdose produces excessive beta-adrenergic stimulation, including tachycardia, arrhythmia, tremor, headache, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, and possible cardiac arrest; discontinue and provide supportive care with cautious cardioselective beta-blockade only when appropriate.
Salmeterol is a LABA for maintenance, not rescue; in asthma it must be paired with an inhaled corticosteroid.
Compared with albuterol, salmeterol has slower onset and roughly 12-hour duration; high-yield toxicities are tremor, tachycardia, hypokalemia, and paradoxical bronchospasm.

statements.text: Sumatriptan is a selective serotonin 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonist. Activation of cranial vascular 5-HT1B receptors and trigeminal 5-HT1D receptors is associated with cranial vasoconstriction and inhibition of pro-inflammatory neuropeptide release.

The therapeutic response reflects suppression of trigeminovascular signaling and constriction of dilated cranial vessels; the same vasoconstrictor pharmacology explains important coronary, cerebral, and peripheral ischemic risks.
Oral tablets abort acute migraine attacks with or without aura in adults; they are not established for migraine prevention or cluster headache.
Subcutaneous injection aborts acute migraine with or without aura and acute cluster headache in adults.
Acute treatment of migraine with or without aura in adults.
Acute treatment of cluster headache in adults.
Common tablet reactions include paresthesia, warm or cold sensations, chest/neck/jaw pressure or tightness, vertigo, and malaise or fatigue.
Common injection reactions include injection-site reactions, tingling, warm or hot sensation, chest discomfort or tightness, pressure sensation, flushing, and dizziness or vertigo.

Serious risks include myocardial ischemia or infarction, coronary vasospasm, life-threatening arrhythmia, stroke or hemorrhage, peripheral or gastrointestinal ischemia, severe hypertension, serotonin syndrome, anaphylaxis, and seizure.
Medication-overuse headache can occur with frequent use of acute migraine drugs and may require withdrawal of the overused medicine.
Clinically important toxicity is dominated by vasospastic and ischemic events, cardiovascular conduction effects, serotonergic toxicity, and hypersensitivity.

The reviewed oral-tablet and subcutaneous-injection labels do not contain a boxed warning; major ischemic, arrhythmic, cerebrovascular, and serotonin-syndrome risks are addressed in Warnings and Precautions.

Contraindications include ischemic coronary disease or coronary vasospasm, Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome or another accessory-pathway arrhythmia, prior stroke or transient ischemic attack, hemiplegic or brainstem-aura migraine, peripheral vascular disease, ischemic bowel disease, and uncontrolled hypertension.

Do not use within 24 hours of another triptan or an ergot-type medicine, within 2 weeks of an MAO-A inhibitor, or in patients with hypersensitivity to sumatriptan; severe hepatic impairment is a contraindication for both the reviewed tablets and subcutaneous injection.
Evaluate triptan-naive patients with multiple cardiovascular risk factors before treatment and consider supervised first dosing with post-dose ECG when the evaluation is negative but risk remains.
Stop treatment and evaluate urgently for suspected cardiac, cerebral, peripheral, or gastrointestinal ischemia, significant arrhythmia, anaphylaxis, serotonin syndrome, or seizure.
Exclude other serious neurologic conditions when headache features are atypical or the diagnosis of migraine or cluster headache is uncertain.
Subcutaneous injection is rapidly absorbed, with a median time to peak concentration of about 12 minutes; oral tablets have a slower onset and should not be treated as dose-equivalent to injection.
The elimination half-life is approximately 2.5 hours after oral tablets and approximately 2 hours after subcutaneous injection.
Sumatriptan is metabolized predominantly by monoamine oxidase A to an inactive indole-acetic-acid metabolite.
After metabolism, drug-related material is eliminated mainly in urine; unchanged renal excretion is a minor route compared with metabolism.
MAO-A inhibitors markedly increase sumatriptan exposure and are contraindicated during treatment and for 2 weeks after discontinuation.
Another triptan or ergot-containing medicine within 24 hours can add vasospastic effects and is contraindicated.
Serotonin syndrome can occur with SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, or MAO inhibitors; monitor for mental-status, autonomic, and neuromuscular findings.

Monitor attack response and frequency of acute-medication use, blood pressure, cardiovascular or neurologic symptoms, and signs of serotonin syndrome; reassess diagnosis when attacks do not respond as expected.
Available pregnancy-registry and observational data are insufficient to establish a drug-associated risk; use only after balancing maternal need and potential fetal risk.
Sumatriptan is excreted in human milk; minimizing infant exposure by avoiding breastfeeding for 12 hours after treatment may be considered.
The effect of renal impairment on sumatriptan pharmacokinetics has not been fully characterized in the reviewed labels; do not infer an evidence-based renal dose from this review.
After oral dosing, mild-to-moderate hepatic impairment increases sumatriptan exposure; the tablet label limits the maximum single dose to 50 mg and contraindicates severe hepatic impairment.

After subcutaneous dosing, mild-to-moderate hepatic impairment did not produce a statistically significant pharmacokinetic difference from healthy controls; severe hepatic impairment was not studied and is contraindicated.
Safety and effectiveness have not been established in pediatric patients for the reviewed tablet or injection products.
Clinical experience in patients 65 years and older is limited; cautious dosing and cardiovascular assessment are appropriate because hepatic, renal, and cardiac function and comorbidity may differ.
There is no specific antidote for overdose; provide supportive care and monitor cardiovascular status for at least 12 hours or while symptoms persist.
Sumatriptan is a 5-HT1B/1D agonist: cranial vasoconstriction plus inhibition of trigeminal neuropeptide release explains both efficacy and ischemic contraindications.
Route pearl: acute cluster headache is a labeled indication for subcutaneous injection, not for the reviewed oral tablet.

statements.text: Trastuzumab binds HER2, inhibits proliferation of HER2-overexpressing tumor cells, and mediates antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.
statements.scope: The reviewed label does not directly state an extracellular subdomain number

statements.text: Therapeutic activity depends on HER2 overexpression or amplification in the tumor; treatment without validated HER2 testing risks exposing patients without a likely target.

In appropriately selected HER2-positive disease, trastuzumab improves clinically important outcomes as adjuvant or metastatic therapy, usually in combination or sequence with other antineoplastic agents.
Adjuvant treatment of HER2-overexpressing node-positive or node-negative high-risk breast cancer in label-specified regimens.
Treatment of HER2-overexpressing metastatic breast cancer as first-line combination therapy with paclitaxel or as single-agent therapy after one or more chemotherapy regimens.
Treatment, with cisplatin and capecitabine or 5-fluorouracil, of HER2-overexpressing metastatic gastric or gastroesophageal-junction adenocarcinoma not previously treated for metastatic disease.

Common reactions vary by regimen and include fever, chills, headache, nausea, diarrhea, infection, cough, rash, fatigue, and infusion-related symptoms; cytopenias are common when combined with myelosuppressive chemotherapy.
Serious risks include cardiomyopathy and heart failure, severe or fatal infusion reactions, pulmonary toxicity, and embryo-fetal harm.
Severe infusion reactions can include anaphylaxis, angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, hypoxia, or acute respiratory distress; delayed deterioration has occurred.
The major organ-system risks are cardiac dysfunction, infusion hypersensitivity, pulmonary injury, and treatment-related fetal toxicity.

Boxed warning: cardiomyopathy, infusion reactions and pulmonary toxicity, and embryo-fetal toxicity. Evaluate left-ventricular function before and during treatment and discontinue or interrupt according to label criteria.
The current HERCEPTIN label lists no formal contraindications; this does not negate the boxed-warning precautions or the need to withhold/discontinue for specified toxicity.
Assess left-ventricular ejection fraction before treatment, at regular intervals during therapy, and after completion as specified; withhold or discontinue for clinically significant decline.
Interrupt infusion for dyspnea or clinically significant hypotension and discontinue for anaphylaxis, angioedema, interstitial pneumonitis, or acute respiratory distress syndrome.
Verify HER2 overexpression or gene amplification using an FDA-approved test before selecting patients.
Trastuzumab has nonlinear, dose-dependent pharmacokinetics and a long terminal persistence; population estimates vary with regimen, disease burden, and body weight.
Trastuzumab elimination is described by parallel linear and nonlinear pathways; the nonlinear pathway has a concentration-dependent clearance that decreases as concentration rises.

Anthracyclines given with or after trastuzumab increase cardiotoxicity. Because trastuzumab can persist in circulation, avoid anthracycline-based therapy for up to 7 months after stopping when possible.

Confirm HER2 overexpression or gene amplification with an FDA-approved test before treatment, then monitor baseline and serial left-ventricular ejection fraction, infusion-reaction symptoms, pulmonary symptoms, and pregnancy status when relevant.
Trastuzumab can cause fetal harm, including oligohydramnios and related complications; advise effective contraception during treatment and for 7 months after the last dose.
Human-milk data are unavailable; consider developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding, maternal need, and the long persistence of trastuzumab.
Population pharmacokinetic analyses did not identify a clinically meaningful effect of mild-to-moderate renal impairment, but data in severe impairment are limited.
The effect of hepatic impairment on trastuzumab pharmacokinetics has not been fully established in the reviewed label.
Safety and effectiveness have not been established in pediatric patients for the reviewed HERCEPTIN indications.
Older patients may have a higher risk of cardiac dysfunction; age and comorbid cardiovascular disease should inform monitoring.

Trastuzumab is a HER2-directed humanized monoclonal antibody that inhibits HER2-overexpressing tumor-cell proliferation and can mediate ADCC; confirm HER2 overexpression or amplification before treatment.
Classic toxicity is cardiomyopathy, especially with anthracyclines; serial LVEF monitoring and the embryo-fetal, infusion, and pulmonary boxed warnings are high yield.

statements.text: Adalimumab is a recombinant human IgG1 monoclonal antibody that binds tumor necrosis factor alpha, blocks interaction with the p55 and p75 TNF receptors, and can lyse cells expressing surface TNF in vitro in the presence of complement.
TNF blockade reduces downstream inflammatory mediators, adhesion molecules, acute-phase reactants, and tissue inflammation across multiple immune-mediated diseases.

Subcutaneous adalimumab reduces signs, symptoms, and structural progression or induces/maintains disease control in label-specified rheumatologic, gastrointestinal, dermatologic, and ophthalmic inflammatory diseases.
Treatment of moderate-to-severe rheumatoid arthritis, polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis under label-specified age and activity criteria.
Treatment of moderate-to-severe Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis in adults and in label-specified pediatric age groups.
Treatment of moderate-to-severe chronic plaque psoriasis, moderate-to-severe hidradenitis suppurativa, and noninfectious intermediate, posterior, or panuveitis under label-specified criteria.
Most common reactions are infections such as upper-respiratory infection or sinusitis, injection-site reactions, headache, and rash.

Serious risks include tuberculosis and other opportunistic or invasive infections, sepsis, malignancy including lymphoma, severe hypersensitivity, hepatitis B reactivation, demyelinating disease, cytopenias, new or worsening heart failure, and lupus-like autoimmunity.

Hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma, a rare and often fatal malignancy, has occurred mainly in adolescent and young-adult males with inflammatory bowel disease receiving TNF blockers, often with azathioprine or mercaptopurine.
Major toxicity domains are infection, malignancy, hypersensitivity, neurologic demyelination, hematologic cytopenia, cardiac failure, hepatic viral reactivation, and autoimmunity.

Boxed warning: increased risk of serious infections leading to hospitalization or death and increased malignancy risk, including lymphoma and hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma in children and adolescents treated with TNF blockers.
The current HUMIRA label lists no formal contraindications; treatment still should not begin during an active infection and must follow the warning-based risk assessment.
Test for latent tuberculosis before and during treatment as clinically indicated; treat latent infection before starting and discontinue or interrupt for serious infection or sepsis.
Screen patients at risk for hepatitis B and monitor carriers during and for several months after therapy because reactivation can be fatal.
Avoid live vaccines and monitor for malignancy, demyelinating symptoms, cytopenia, heart failure, hypersensitivity, and lupus-like syndrome.
The mean terminal half-life is approximately 2 weeks, with reported values of about 10 to 20 days.
The mean terminal half-life is approximately 2 weeks and mean apparent clearance is about 12 mL/hour; anti-adalimumab antibodies can increase apparent clearance.
Combining adalimumab with anakinra, abatacept, another TNF blocker, or another biologic used for the same condition can increase serious infection risk and is not recommended.
Avoid live vaccines during treatment; non-live vaccines may be given, although immune responses can be attenuated.

Because chronic inflammation can suppress CYP formation, starting or stopping HUMIRA may alter exposure of narrow-therapeutic-index CYP substrates; monitor therapeutic effect or drug concentration and adjust the substrate when needed.

Monitor baseline and interval tuberculosis risk, active or opportunistic infection, hepatitis B status when at risk, complete blood count when clinically indicated, heart-failure symptoms, neurologic findings, skin cancer, and disease response.
Available human pregnancy data do not reliably establish a drug-associated risk; placental transfer increases later in pregnancy and can affect timing of live vaccines in exposed infants.
Limited data show low concentrations in human milk; weigh breastfeeding benefits, maternal need, and potential infant effects.
No formal pharmacokinetic studies were conducted in renal impairment; the reviewed label does not provide a renal dose adjustment.
No formal pharmacokinetic studies were conducted in hepatic impairment; evaluate liver disease and hepatitis B risk clinically rather than inferring a labeled dose adjustment.

Pediatric use is established for selected juvenile idiopathic arthritis, Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, hidradenitis suppurativa, and uveitis populations; age and weight thresholds are indication-specific.
Serious infection and malignancy risks may be greater in older adults; use particular caution and monitor closely.
Doses up to 10 mg/kg were administered in clinical trials without evidence of dose-limiting toxicity; monitor patients for adverse reactions after excessive exposure.

statements.text: Atezolizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds PD-L1 and blocks its interactions with PD-1 and B7.1, releasing PD-L1-mediated inhibition of antitumor T-cell responses without inducing antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.
PD-L1 blockade can restore antitumor immune activity but also disrupt peripheral immune tolerance, explaining immune-mediated toxicity in essentially any organ system.
Intravenous atezolizumab provides checkpoint-inhibitor activity as monotherapy or in label-specified combinations for selected solid tumors defined by disease stage, biomarkers, and prior therapy.
Treatment of label-specified non-small-cell lung cancer populations, including adjuvant and metastatic settings selected by tumor stage, PD-L1 status, driver alterations, and prior treatment.

For extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer, TECENTRIQ is indicated with carboplatin and etoposide for first-line treatment; after induction with TECENTRIQ or atezolizumab and hyaluronidase plus carboplatin and etoposide without disease progression, TECENTRIQ with lurbinectedin is an indicated maintenance regimen.

Additional label-specified indications include unresectable or metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma, BRAF V600-mutated melanoma in combination therapy, unresectable or metastatic alveolar soft-part sarcoma from age 2 years, and adjuvant treatment after cystectomy for adults with muscle-invasive bladder cancer and ctDNA-detected molecular residual disease.
statements.scope: Indication-specific stage, biomarker, age, and combination limits

statements.text: Common adverse reactions vary by indication and combination and include fatigue or asthenia, decreased appetite, nausea, cough or dyspnea, diarrhea, constipation, rash, pyrexia, musculoskeletal pain, and laboratory abnormalities.

Severe or fatal immune-mediated reactions can involve the lungs, colon, liver, endocrine organs, kidneys, skin, nervous system, heart, blood, eyes, or other tissues; serious infusion reactions and complications after allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplant also occur.
Rare immune toxicities include myocarditis, myositis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, myasthenic syndromes, encephalitis, severe cutaneous reactions, hemolytic anemia, and aplastic anemia.
Toxicity is predominantly immune-mediated and multisystem, with additional infusion-reaction, transplant-related, and embryo-fetal risks.
The current TECENTRIQ label does not contain a boxed warning; severe and fatal immune-mediated toxicities are detailed under Warnings and Precautions.

The current TECENTRIQ label lists no formal contraindications; eligibility and treatment interruption are instead governed by indication, immune toxicity, infusion reactions, and combination-regimen restrictions.

Identify suspected immune-mediated toxicity early, exclude alternative causes including infection, and withhold or permanently discontinue according to severity; systemic corticosteroids or other immunosuppression may be required.
Monitor for infusion reactions and interrupt, slow, or discontinue infusion according to severity.
Fatal and serious complications can occur in patients receiving allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation before or after PD-1/PD-L1 blockade.
The terminal half-life is approximately 27 days at steady state.
The mean clearance at steady state is approximately 0.2 L/day; the reviewed label does not directly attribute elimination to a named protein-catabolic, renal, or CYP pathway.

At baseline and periodically during treatment, monitor liver enzymes, creatinine, and thyroid function and assess for pulmonary, gastrointestinal, endocrine, neurologic, cardiac, dermatologic, hematologic, ocular, and infusion-related symptoms.
Use the label-specified biomarker or molecular testing and disease-stage criteria when patient selection requires them.
Based on mechanism of action, atezolizumab can cause fetal harm; advise effective contraception during treatment and for 5 months after the last dose.
Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions, breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment and for 5 months after the last dose.
Population pharmacokinetic analyses did not identify a clinically significant effect of mild or moderate renal impairment; data in severe renal impairment are limited.
Mild or moderate hepatic impairment had no clinically significant effect on atezolizumab pharmacokinetics; the effect of severe hepatic impairment is unknown.

Safety and effectiveness are established for unresectable or metastatic alveolar soft-part sarcoma in pediatric patients 2 years and older; other reviewed indications are not established in pediatric patients.

For the TECENTRIQ plus lurbinectedin maintenance regimen, patients aged 65 years and older had more grade 3 or 4 adverse reactions and more treatment discontinuations than younger patients; this finding should not be generalized to every atezolizumab regimen.
Atezolizumab binds PD-L1 and blocks its interactions with PD-1 and B7.1, releasing PD-L1-mediated inhibition of antitumor T-cell responses.
Checkpoint blockade can cause immune-mediated disease in almost any organ; high-yield monitoring includes lungs, bowel, liver, endocrine glands, kidneys, skin, and neurologic/cardiac systems.
